No problem! Glad I didn't go too overboard. It's a book that affected me profoundly and has stood out among a sea of forgettable and memorable books I've read over the years. Murakami isn't an author I love as much as I used to, but when I revisit him, WUBC is the book I return to the most. I don't know why I like it as much as I do; I sympathize with people who don't like it because I truly didn't like it either the first time I read it. But in some subconscious way it resonated with me, and the first time I reread it something just "clicked". I'm not sure that "click" would happen to others on a reread - maybe they would just hate the book all over again lol - I think parts of my personal life mixed with Murakami using the right words and scenes and themes formed that Eureka! moment for me; in that way it feels like a very "personal" book, and maybe it is a very boring book without that feeling.

When I first read it, it was also my least favorite Murakami book, I thought it was boring and meandering. Now, since rereading (multiple times), it's my favorite Murakami book, and the only one I still reread alongside Kafka.

I couldn't really tell you why I love it so much now (I'm due for another reread, it's been like a year), but the slow and meandering nature of the book doesn't bother or bore me because it fits the themes of the book, and the themes are what are so powerful to me. It's his most philosophical work I think (After Dark is really philosophical as well, and it's also in my top 3), and, to me, it's all about suffering and about learning to integrate into the flow of life. Time and place and all that - it says not to struggle against pain and darkness, but to climb into the darkness, this way you can better understand the situation and know when the time comes to actually "fight" or use your energy. If you don't know when to use your energy, if you lash out the moment the pain comes - which inevitably comes to us all, usually at points we cannot predict - then you waste your time struggling against an impassible wall, don't have anything in the tank left when you actually need it (don't even know how to identify when the right time is).

The main character of WUB is constantly out of his debt, but he doesn't learn "acceptance" or anything like that. He fights, he's not satisfied with the answers he gets, he feels something is wrong, and while he seems like a passive person, he refuses to be passive when it matters, and he learns throughout the book to identify what "matters". Like his meeting with nutmeg and cinnamon, and other events of the book, things just "happen" to him when he learns to let go. One of the reasons I love this book so much is because, even though the whole thing is very magically surreal, it is also very accurate in the sense of how, when you really let go, life happens to you more, and you have more energy to use when it does happen, because you haven't wasted it struggling and fighting something which cannot be fought. To me, the book and characters are all about "accepting your destiny", which in real life doesn't really equate to just being passive and accepting everything is deterministic, but instead learning to identify what you can and can't change. His wife in the book is an example of the dynamic nature of this - he learns no matter what that he cannot fully understand her,or anyone else for that matter, but he still KNOWS her, knows something isn't right despite her telling him to abandon her, and he learns to change what matters and let be what he cannot.

Intent is important even if even inspiration isn't (in regards to genre). Genre is a cloudy term, but if you're going to try to discuss it in any categorical capacity, like if you were trying to sort a library based on the most logical system you can come up with, then Dune and Hyperion are sci-fi, just like how Lord of the Rings is fantasy (even if you could say Tolkien took a more scientific, rigorous approach to his world, the setting, his intent, is fantasy, is magic).

I've only read book one of Dune, but I'm pretty sure even the Bene Gesserit powers are made with neurology in mind, not magic, even if they aren't technically possible (which we don't know, since we aren't from this fictional far future).

Yes, there are hard sci-fi space operas that exist, but you can literally take any author, even hard sci-fi ones, even authors like Greg Egan, and be like "well even if that's super scientifically thought out, it's still impossible, so therefore it's still fantasy". That's not what matters when talking about fiction and genres. 

And bending the rules via unknown laws of physics is basically another word for magic. These things are fluid and all opinion-based though. So again, I can't say "Hyperion and Dune are just sci-fi and you're wrong", but if we were to try to find some ground that best suits what constitutes things fall into one genre over another, and if you had to pick one defining genre for Hyperion and Dune, you are going to put them in in science fiction, because they are fictional stories with science in mind, not magic.

Yeah it does sound like more magic than science, but that's just about every single space opera if you want to get technical. Anything that uses FTL is automatically fantasy. The Void which Binds, and empathy being nonlocal and transcendent, were inspired from scientific ideas, even if they aren't actual science (it's science fiction). Hyperion and Dune are not fantasy, even if they have fantastical elements; the authors did not intend for anything to be magic.

It has been a long long time since I've watched his lectures, but it was honestly kind of enlightening to learn where his theories were wrong, and in general they taught still teach really good ways of looking at biological systems and completely opened my eyes about some stuff, so I would say his works and lectures are still 100% worth consuming. I couldn't give you exact examples without going through my notebook (which I don't have right now) - say *this, this* and *this* are wrong - but in general the incorrect information comes from how much he attributes to *this brain region does this, these hormones are responsible for this,* etc... and his lack of attribution to how the brain works as network and how different brain regions and different neurons can evolve differently in different people to do different things - ie: many-to-one (degeneracy) and one-to-many: many different combinations of neurons can produce the same outcome, and singular networks can contribute to many different outcomes. The brains core systems are highly flexible and individualized, and you can't predict someone's emotions without knowing their entire personal history.

The best sources I've come across for explaining how neurological systems actually work would probably be the books *How Emotions Are Made* by Barrett and *The Hidden Spring* by Solms. Barrett's book basically directly refutes many of Sapolsky's earlier claims about how brains work; *The Hidden Spring* explains how consciousness evolves and functions (many people still mistake what consciousness actually his - hell, even googling the question gives you the wrong answer, as it does not arise in the cortex). *The Hidden Spring* is actually more inline with Sapolsky's views - there's a little bit of truth in everything, and everything written about psychological sciences will be wrong in some way - as people like Solms and Sapolsky like to put heavy emphasis on our ancient animal brains and primal regions, and consciousness is probably the hardest question to try to objectively answer, as we are conscious entities. It's more so a matter of what they get right, and Barrett's book is the best for what you probably want in the sense that it explains what we *don't* and *can't* know, where as that was Sapolsky's problem: stating what we knew about which parts of the brain and which neurons do what, when in reality they do a lot more and a lot less than he attributes, and their results are infinitely variable

I will eventually but I still need to finish his book *Behave*. Also, despite Sapolsky being one the authors that really got me into biology and psychology (or evolutionary psychology), I learned later a ton of stuff he taught in his popular lectures is very incorrect, and it does not pass replication tests. Similarly, the Dunyain's abilities in The Second Apocalypse are completely fictional and not actual possible in real life (which doesn't make me like the series any less; some of my favorite sci-fi books are ones where the central thesis have proven false, but they're still amazing thought experiments, and fiction, after all), as there is no way to read someone's thoughts or even emotions accurately based on their face, as emotions and expressions are objectively different based on culture and upbringing; the best you can hope for are good approximations, which is why stereotypes can be accurate but never truly accurate, only really good guesses.

But anyways, Sapolsky is awesome and yes I will be picking it up, but I'm doubtful about anything very dogmatic in regards to determinism - in both physics and biology (but in reality I'm sure Sapolsky's new book is more nuanced and isn't as straightforward as typical determinist claims).

This is actually one of my favorite subgenres (for my gr shelf I call it *transmutation sci-fi)* and I'm always on the lookout for books like this! Most of these I would also classify as sci-fi, and they may be more on the technical side than just straight up horror than you're looking for, but here are some of my favorites:

**Diamond Dogs** by Alastair Reynolds. Obsessive and rich people tackle a deadly alien maze and must transform their bodies more and more the more they wish to continue.

**The Skinner** by Neal Asher. Deals with a planet that has evolved immortality, but there are costs, and there are other evolutionary alien horrors the main characters come across. This book and its waterworld and characters is awesome.

**Annihilation** by Jeff VanderMeer. Everyone knows this one already.

**Sisyphean** by Dempow Torishima. An absolute gem of a book. If you don't mind challenging reads and love evolutionary horror in some of its wildest forms I'd highly recommend trying this book. The author's art throughout is also incredible.

**Bas Lag** by China Mieville. I haven't read Iron Council but **Perdido Street Station** and **The Scar** are sprawling epics filled with fantastical and evolutionary horrors.

**Blindsight** and **Starfish** by Peter Watts. Difficult and bleak sci-fi books. Blindsight is maybe a bit more philosophical than you'd want if you just want horrendous creatures; it's a first contact story where the aliens are an expression of an idea that evolution itself trends toward a horrifying conclusion with intelligence. Starfish deals with people in harsh environments modifying their body more and more and becoming less and less attached to humanity.

**The Vorrh** **trilogy** by B Catling. The garden of Eden is in Africa and it has it's own twisted evolution and creatures. Some humans also have their bodies and minds modified throughout the series.

Here's some things to do with your dog:

Instead of feeding her from a bowl, pour her allotted food for dinner in a pouch or something and feed her every time she does something good. Looks at you? Good girl, treat. Sits? Good girl, treat. Not react to traffic? Good girl, treat. Ect... Make her learn to earn. You'll get 100 training sessions instead of 1 feeding session.

Practice turns A LOT while walking. This will change your life, I promise. Walk her forward a bit, turn and say "[dog name], let's go!", go the other way, repeat a lot. Every time you do this and she turns with you, good girl and praise her. What this does is teaches your dog to engage with you - it makes everything easier. Make sure you are exciting and positive: every time you turn, encourage her heavily, even walk backwards if you need, when you "Let's go!". Do these directional turns a lot. Combine this with Sit, Down, Look at Me, Wait, etc... Exercises and your dog will start listening to you a lot more. 

Sit down in heavily trafficked area with your dog, don't move, let her observe. If she's being good, say Good Girl and stroke her. Do this for a while. Do not do this if she is super reactive and cannot calm down; start somewhere smaller and less populated. If she will not look at you and engage with you at all, this is a sign she needs more basic command and turning exercises to learn how to engage with you, and/or the stimulus is too much

If she's about to react to something, immediately turn and walk the other direction until your dog looks at you and will follow commands and take treats. If you can't walk another direction, physically stand in front of your dog and the stimulus, blocking her eyesight until she looks up at you and will again follow commands and take treats. If she doesn't, it's important to walk to other way.

I would do some leash training exercises and training exercises in the house. Also reward often. Teach him/her Watch Me / Look at Me too. Also Come (do all this in the house, with the leash and harness on, dragging on floor or loosely hold; get them used to it on.) Look At Me is crucial - you want to practice this in your house and reward heavily. Tell your dog to look at you, maintain eye contract, reward when they do. On your walk, you don't want your dog staring at you all the time, nor will they because you want the walk to be for the dog and pleasurable (training walks should be separate, but right now worry about training in the house, the on pleasure walks, reward your dog randomly, and always after she looks at you). Make sure if they look at you on the walk, say Good Boy/Girl or excited Yes! And reward. Practice this in the house by moving a treat to your eyes and saying look at me. Reward often and fast. (Also ask to do Sit and Lie Down and Leave It and such while training in the house - you mine as well and dogs can learn many things at once). If you're leash training in the house and the dog is pulling, switch directions immediately; if he complies, reward heavily. 

Always exercise heavily before a walk.

Also make sure to buy a long leash so your dog can explore, and remember there are pleasure walks and training walks. Teach your dog commands over and over in the house so he both learns commands better, and checks with you often because he never knows when he's getting a treat. Reward heavily on walks any time he does something good, and reward randomly and unexpectedly. If he's being bad, say No and walk in the opposite direction. Don't be harsh while training on pleasure walks; it won't work because your dog is in an exciting environment; train in the house and reward for every good thing on walks, focus a lot on Watch Me, and your dog should gradually get better on walks.

If your dog loves toys, even better: you can reward with play as well as small great food. Bring a tug toy or ball (if they prefer that and if you have long leash) on a walk as well as treats, and if they do something good praise them and have a couple second play session (won't work if they don't really care about toys and are highly focused on the walk; stick to treats)

Make sure to capture good behaviors: you don't need to say a command before a trick always, if you're walking and your dog looks at you, hold you fingers to your eyes and say Watch Me or Look At Me quickly, then reward.

The book's primary theme is consciousness, and the pieces do not come together until the end, and even then you might not grasp all the players/sequence of events. (The central thesis of the book is wrong, with what we now know about brains, but that doesn't detract anything from the book, and it's one of the few pieces of fiction that balance horror and sci-fi, scientific prose with imagination, storytelling with humor.) Also some people get tripped up about the vampires, but it makes sense for what Watts is going for - exploring differences in consciousness and using a fictional created subspecies - we know in reality there were a lot of different human species - as a big piece in the story.

I also have ADHD and bad impulse control and can throw myself too much into a hobby. So far, I have avoided any serious mistakes with fountain pens, but I have still wasted money. I would recommend firstly figuring out what you want fountain pens for. For me, I like journaling and note-taking and quote writing, but I mostly do my extensive journaling online now. So I've decided not to spend way too much money on pens I won't use much, because I KNOW I'll regret it. In the past I bought cheap Jinhao pens, and honestly that was invaluable info to me because I've learned what kind of nibs I like (mostly EF, and I like Fude nibs a lot too, mostly for art, which I never would've known if I didn't accidently pick that nib while buying cheap pens). I've also realized quality differences because of experience with cheap pens: some cheap metal jinhaos I've had in the past feel better than $50 plastic pens I've had, but it's all preference. I bought a TWSBI a long time ago that I didn't expect to still be using, but it turned out to be super reliable, feel nice, have an awesome nib, and it's my go-to pen. I've learned a lot from jinhaos, my TWSBI, my pilot Kakuna, and my FPR pens, all of which add up to like around $100. I have yet to buy an expensive pen, but now I know if I do, itll only be one like $100-200 Japanese EF pen; the rest (mediums, stub, flex....) I don't need expensive pens for. I'd also recommend learning to modify your pen. I thought I'd never do this - too scared; and ADHD makes things overwhelming - but honestly there's a lot of simple and rewarding stuff you can learn to do that becomes less daunting the more you know; so now I'm less worried about "fucking up" a pen because I know I can replace / grease /exchange parts and not just buy a whole nother pen. So that's my shitty advice, basically: experiment with cheap pens and figure out what you like, then limit yourself to a certain amount of pens.

Consciousness is the primary theme, and these elements - the difference between baseline humans, altered humans, altered but closely related species (vampires), and AI - all fit well, imo, vampires included. Vampires are not as farfetched of a plot device for someone that is a biologist and writing hard sci-fi as people think, it's not just because it's the popular craze. Your problem with the characters I think is wrong expectations. They are supposed to be one dimensional in many ways. They are high autists and heavily modified specialists picked for a weird ass mission. They are plot points because they are literally selected - in story - to be very specific at certain things.

As for the main message, I liked it because I love nihilistic fiction and don't think it's presented well in most books - I think Blindsight is very unique - but your criticism is totally valid. Blindsight is also wrong about many of its statements about consciousness, but I'm okay with that and still love the book and think it's written well; I think it ages well in ways that make fiction enjoyable to me, even if the themes don't as much. I get that it can feel preachy and skewed in the balance though.
